newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Autralia Oct jobs may speed RBA easing cycle.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Autralia Oct jobs may speed RBA easing cycle.

text.p: Australian employment is generally expected to have bounced back in October after a steep drop the month before, but not by nearly enough to dent the stubbornly high unemployment rate.

Median forecasts for the Thursday data favoured a modest 12,000 rise in jobs, but that was only a third of the 34,100 fall registered in September and would leave the jobless total unchanged at 8.7 percent.
The data may be pre-empted somewhat by the Reserve Bank which is widely expected to cut rates Wednesday, but could still be crucial as a signpost to the future course of policy.

"Soft employment data on top of other recent releases will add to pressure on the RBA for a rate cut, if they have not already moved, and spark speculation about further cuts if they have," said local brokerage firm Bain and Co, the Australian arm of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The RBA board holds its monthly meeting on Tuesday and most analysts feel it will sanction a 0.50 point reduction in official rates to 6.5 percent.
Bain was by far the most bearish about the employment data, having revised their forecast for employment to a 10,000-20,000 fall on Monday from an original 20,000 rise.

"We've had a close look at the seasonal factors affecting employment and taken into account the surprising weakness of retail sales, which has in the past biased the jobs numbers downwards," said Ivan Colhoun, an associate director at Bain.
"And we think the balance of risk is for another soft result in October and no bounce until November."
Retail sales data last week showed trade plunged 3.7 percent in September against market forecasts of a 0.5 percent dip.
Bain also pointed to the 1.0 percent fall in ANZ job advertisements in October, the fourth monthly drop in a row, as proof the labour market was lifeless at the moment.
If Bain was right, the unemployment rate could hit the politically sensitive 9.0 percent level for the first time since January 1995.
Such an outcome could convince the market, at least, that more than one easing was in the pipeline given the RBA's emphasis on unemployment when it cut rates on July 31 this year.

Then the central bank noted its charter gave it responsibility for reducing unemployment as well as inflation and with the latter contained, the economy could run a little faster without too much risk.

"Even if the RBA does go on Wednesday, you can only ignore the employment numbers at your own risk," said Tim Moloney, an economist at Commonwealth Bank. "If they're weak again the market will certainly start factoring in more than one easing."
The majority of analysts were not as pessimistic as Bain on employment for October -- estimates ranged as high as a 25,000 rise -- but all agreed the outlook was a sober one.

"We're not convinced there's a link between retail sales and employment, so we tend to think jobs growth will return to its trend of around 10,000 to 15,000," said Stephen Ryan, an economist at St George Bank.

But he noted that the latest detailed data on the labour market in the September quarter, which was released last week, suggested the downtrend in long term unemployment had bottomed and showed early signs of turning up once more.
"That's important because it represents the level of structural unemployment in the economy and that is what the RBA and the government having been trying so hard, for so long to improve," said Ryan.
